correctness.rationale: Reconstructed the Cartier calculation and polynomial proof in RESULT.md §§1–6. The parity and degree cutoffs leave precisely the two indicated coefficients (with inverse Frobenius); at smooth coefficients their zero loci coincide. The Lucas digit comparison gives vanishing through derivative order m at ±2. Dividing by (u²−4)^(m+1) gives the lower-degree ODE with a unique solution up to scale because neither recurrence factor vanishes below degree m. At a smooth root the same ODE excludes multiplicity at least two since m<p. The elliptic and Prym statements use the invariant and anti-invariant blocks under a prime-to-p isogeny. Normalizing b=1 leaves sign as the only scaling identification, so the class count follows by parity. At p=5 the divisor is empty (the formula's second branch is not realized). Inspected the supporting verifier without executing it; its finite multinomial and squarefreeness checks are not an all-prime proof.

evidence: Write b=q², a=q u, z=q w. Then [z^d](z²+az+b)^N=q^(2N−d)[w^d](w²+uw+1)^N. Applying this to N=4m+3 and 2m+1 lifts the prior V_m identity and contributes exactly b^(m+1)(a²−4b)^(m+1). For the count, sign exchanges the nonzero roots in pairs and fixes exactly zero when m is odd, by the coefficient parity and squarefreeness.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Neither the literal b-variable restatement nor the count of marked classes needs a new structural lemma beyond the indexed result and known marked scaling. The elliptic/Prym separation follows from the same Cartier blocks and prime-to-p decomposition.

evidence: The indexed record sets R_m(a)=[t^m](t²+at+1)^(2m+1) and explicitly equates it with [t^(3m+2)] of the same polynomial. Its Proof gives V_m=K_m(a²−4)^(m+1)R_m with K_m=binom(4m+3,3m+2)/binom(2m+1,m).
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The reciprocal exponents sum to 4m+2, so R_m is exactly H_m(a,1), and binomial symmetry gives K_m=c_m. No change of prime or of smooth parameter locus is involved.

The full b-dependent formula is its weighted homogenization, and the marked orbit count is an immediate consequence of the earlier parity polynomial and the known scaling law.
